did_you_know.text: The psalm’s title calls it a “song,” or “psalm song,” and attributes it to David; the title does not specify the event for which it was composed.
The psalm presents God as the “Father of orphans” and “Judge of widows”—that is, as the protector of orphans and the judge who cares for widows.
The verse contrasts God, who gives the solitary a home and leads prisoners out, with the rebellious, who remain in a parched land.
God’s appearance is described in the context of the people’s exodus and journey through the wilderness, and the next verse explicitly mentions Sinai and the God of Israel.
The rain is called “rain of bounty” and is described as a blessing that waters and establishes the inheritance and the weary people.
The verse describes God’s word as good news, and the women who proclaim it as a “great host”—a phrase emphasizing the large number of those spreading the news.
The verse uses the image of a dove whose wings are covered with silver and whose feathers gleam like greenish gold—a poetic picture of splendor and radiance.
The mountains of Bashan are described as “many-peaked mountains,” but the psalm emphasizes that the mountain God desired as his dwelling is the mountain where the Lord will dwell forever.
God’s chariot is described in terms of myriads and thousands upon thousands, and the verse connects it with Sinai and the sanctuary.
God’s procession is depicted as a musical procession: singers lead the way, musicians follow, and young women play tambourines; the tribes of Israel are also mentioned later.
